summary: Describes Media Server Control Markup Language, used with SIP to provide advanced conferencing and interactive voice response functions. It offers an application-level control model, such as between a conference focus and mixer. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: MSCML is an XML language for sending conference and phone-menu commands to a media server through SIP. The RFC is Informational, and its IESG note says it was not reviewed as a candidate Internet Standard.

questions: how does mscml control a media server
what is the mscml conference control leg
how does mscml use sip info
subtitle: XML payloads for controlling conferences and interactive voice response through SIP.

tldr.problem: Basic SIP call operations do not provide all the controls needed for enhanced conferencing and interactive voice response.
tldr.mechanism: Media Server Control Markup Language (MSCML) carries one XML request in a SIP INVITE or INFO. A media server processes conference, participant, prompt, digit-collection, and recording commands and returns responses or notifications.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5022 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 4722. Its IESG note says it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard and advises caution when evaluating it for implementation or deployment.

today: RFC 5022 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 4722. Its IESG note says it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What MSCML Controls
sections.content:
Media Server Control Markup Language (MSCML) defines XML payloads that a client sends to a media server using SIP INVITE and INFO requests. It covers advanced conferencing and interactive voice response (IVR).

Conference commands configure conferences, change participant legs, and request event reports. IVR commands play media, collect telephone keypad digits, and record media. The RFC describes MSCML as an application-level control model using conferences and call legs.
sections.plainLanguage: An application sends XML commands to a media server through SIP. The commands control conferences or ask the server to play, collect, or record media.

sections.title: SIP Requests and the MSCML Message Model
sections.content:
MSCML can appear in SIP INVITE or INFO requests. Mid-call commands use INFO. The RFC allows only one MSCML body in a SIP request and one request or response in each body; the XML has top-level request, response, and notification elements.

A client can include an identifier to match a request with its response. MSCML uses the SIP dialog to identify which call or conference a command concerns. The media server returns responses and notifications in SIP INFO messages.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIP dialog identifies the call or conference that a command affects. Each XML body contains one request, response, or notification.

sections.title: Conference Control and Participant Legs
sections.content:
The advanced conference model uses an application server as the conference focus and a media server as the mixer. The first INVITE for a conference identifier creates the conference. If it carries a configure_conference request, its dialog becomes the Conference Control Leg.

The conference lasts as long as its control leg. A BYE on that leg ends the participant legs as well. Clients can configure individual legs with settings such as full, mute, parked, preferred, or private. Personalized audio mixes use team relationships between legs.
sections.plainLanguage: A control leg manages the conference as a whole, while each participant leg can have its own settings. Ending the control leg also ends the remaining participant legs.

sections.title: IVR Prompts, Digits, and Recording
sections.content:
The IVR service supports playing announcements, collecting DTMF digits, and recording. Its main requests are play, playcollect, and playrecord. IVR payloads travel in INFO requests, and the media server does not queue them: a new request stops an operation already in progress.

A prompt can include audio files and spoken variables. A playcollect request can play a prompt and collect digits, with configurable timers and special keys. The default first-digit timer is 5000 ms; the default escape and return keys are star and pound. A client can request that collected digits be omitted from server logs.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can play a prompt, collect keypad entries, or record media. A new IVR command stops the current operation rather than waiting in a queue.

sections.title: Security and Publication Status
sections.content:
The RFC says the media server must protect session integrity, confidentiality, and security, and must prevent one participant from accessing another conference without authorization. It requires support for SIPS and TLS because collected information can be sensitive, and recommends support for Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP).

The RFC also contains an IESG note: it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard, publication was at the RFC Editor's discretion, and readers should exercise caution when evaluating it for implementation or deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Media servers must prevent unauthorized access to conference sessions and protect sensitive collected information. The IESG note says this RFC was not reviewed as a candidate Internet Standard.
